turns.content: I need help drafting a short message to my uncle Tarek letting him know I'll come for dessert only on Sunday (if that's still possible without making it weird). Two days ago I lost my temper with Aunt Salma and called her a bitter old woman — which I feel awful about, honestly — but she's been mocking my panic disorder for months and I'm convinced she pushed me on purpose so my uncles would think I'm unstable and sideline me from the building decisions. I'm not boycotting the lunch or starting a family war, but I'm not pretending everything's fine either. Can you help me with the wording?

You can keep it warm and clear without explaining the whole conflict or guessing at Salma’s motives:

“Hi Uncle Tarek, if it still works, I’d like to come just for dessert on Sunday. I regret what I said to Aunt Salma, but I’m still upset about what led up to it and need a little space. I’m not trying to make a statement by missing lunch—I’d still like to see you all. Would that be okay?”

You can regret the insult without pretending the comments about your panic disorder were okay. I’d leave the building decisions out of this message so it stays about Sunday.

That draft is close (though "still upset about what led up to it" feels a bit vague — like I'm hiding the real issue, which might make them wonder more). I'm also worried Tarek will just pressure me to come for the full meal once I'm there for dessert, and I'm not sure how to preempt that in a message without sounding combative (which I really don't want to be). Can I add a line saying I'd rather not discuss the conflict at lunch, or would that provoke the exact conversation I'm trying to avoid?

Yes—you can add that boundary. It might prompt a question, but it also makes your wishes clear in advance. Since you’ll only be there for dessert, I’d say **“on Sunday”** rather than “at lunch,” and name the hurtful comments without speculating about Salma’s intentions.

“Hi Uncle Tarek, would it still work for me to join you just for dessert on Sunday? I regret what I said to Aunt Salma. Her comments about my panic disorder have been hurtful, though, and I need a little space. I’d like to see everyone, but I’ll be keeping it to dessert and would rather leave the disagreement for another time. Let me know what time to come.”

That asks whether the arrangement works without making **dessert only** sound like an opening offer. If he pushes for the full meal, you can repeat, warmly: “Thanks, but dessert is what I’m comfortable with this Sunday. I hope that still works.”

Right — that wording is better, but I’m picturing Tarek reading "her comments about my panic disorder have been hurtful" and immediately thinking I’m fragile (which is kind of his default assumption already). If I say it that plainly, won’t it just confirm his view that I can’t handle family dynamics?

Naming what bothered you doesn’t mean you can’t handle family dynamics. But you can’t control how Tarek interprets it, and you don’t need to explain the conflict in order to set a limit for Sunday.

If you want to name the issue without focusing on how it made you feel, **“I’m not okay with the jokes about my panic disorder”** is more direct. For example:

“Hi Uncle Tarek, if it still works, I’d like to come just for dessert on Sunday. I regret what I said to Aunt Salma, but I’m not okay with the jokes about my panic disorder. I’d still like to see everyone, so I’ll join you after lunch, and I’d prefer to discuss the disagreement another time—not at the gathering. What time would be good for dessert?”

Arriving **after lunch** also does more to protect your dessert-only plan than explaining why you don’t want the full meal. You can take responsibility for the insult without treating the ongoing mockery as acceptable.

My mother just came down to tell me that if I don't apologize unconditionally and attend the full lunch, I'm proving that I can't handle family relationships (which stings, because she's not wrong that I lost my temper, but she's also acting like Salma's months of mocking didn't happen). She said she's not taking sides, but her whole pitch is basically that I should absorb the conflict to keep peace — and that feels like taking a side, doesn't it? How do I hold my boundary without making her feel like I'm forcing her to choose between me and her sister-in-law?

I can see why that stings. You’ve acknowledged that the insult was wrong; being told that only a full lunch will prove you can handle relationships turns a specific mistake into a judgment about your character.

**Your mother may see herself as keeping the peace, but the solution she’s proposing puts the burden of restoring it on you.** That doesn’t necessarily mean she endorses Salma’s comments, but it makes sense that it doesn’t feel neutral.

You don’t have to get her to agree she’s taking a side. Instead, separate what you’re taking responsibility for from what you’re asking her to respect:

“Mum, I’m not asking you to choose between me and Salma or to argue with her for me. Calling her that was wrong, and I can apologize for it without excuses. But apologizing and attending the full lunch are separate things. I’m willing to come for dessert, and I’m not willing to come for the whole meal this Sunday. You don’t have to agree with that decision, but please respect it.”

If she repeats that this proves you can’t handle family relationships:

“I know you’re worried about the family. I’m taking responsibility for what I said and choosing a shorter visit so I can participate calmly. I don’t want to keep debating what that says about me.”

And an apology can be unconditional **about the insult** without becoming blanket acceptance of everything that happened:

“Aunt Salma, I’m sorry I called you a bitter old woman. It was disrespectful, and I shouldn’t have said it.”

You can address the mocking separately, another time. **Owning your behavior doesn’t require surrendering your boundary.** You can reassure your mother that you aren’t asking her to choose; you can’t guarantee she won’t still feel uncomfortable with your decision.

She just posted in the family group chat — a photo of the ladder from the courtyard with the caption "hope nobody slips on the way to the property meeting" (which is clearly aimed at me, since I'm the one who mentioned that ladder needed fixing before the next building vote). Do I respond now to call out the dig, or wait until I see her at dessert on Sunday and address it in person (if at all)?

**I wouldn’t call it out in the group chat right now—or save up a confrontation for dessert.** There’s a third option: address the ladder as a practical issue, and decide separately whether the comment needs a response.

Given the history and your earlier repair request, I understand why it feels aimed at you. But the caption alone doesn’t establish her intent. A public argument could pull attention away from the repair and toward another dispute about your reaction.

If the safety issue needs a reply, keep it factual:

“Thanks for flagging the ladder. That’s the one I raised as needing repair. Can we confirm who’s arranging that before the meeting?”

Otherwise, you can leave the post unanswered. **Not responding isn’t agreeing with it or giving up your voice in the building decisions.**

You also don’t need to turn Sunday into the discussion you’ve already said you don’t want. If she makes a direct remark then:

“I’m happy to discuss the ladder repair at the property meeting. I’m not discussing our disagreement here.”

For now, step away from the chat long enough to choose a response rather than feel pushed into one. Keep your dessert plan separate from this post.
